title: Natural Resources Defense Council v. EPA (1981)
shortTitle: Natural Resources Defense Council v. EPA (1981) — diesel technology note
summary: EPA may set a technology forcing emission standard on a prediction that a control device will be perfected in time, so long as it answers theoretical objections, identifies the remaining development steps, and gives plausible reasons why each can be completed before the deadline.
notes:
Key line: "The Clean Air Act requires the EPA to look to the future in setting standards, but the agency must also provide a reasoned explanation of its basis for believing that its projection is reliable." (Mikva, J.)

Citation: 655 F.2d 318 (D.C. Cir. 1981).

sections.Parties: The Natural Resources Defense Council petitioned for review, arguing that EPA's diesel emission standards were too lax. General Motors Corporation petitioned separately, arguing that the standards were too strict and technologically infeasible; Mercedes-Benz of North America and Volkswagen of America intervened on the industry side and Mercedes-Benz also petitioned. The respondents were the Environmental Protection Agency and its Administrator, Douglas M. Costle. Automobiles Peugeot intervened in support of the NOx waivers. The consolidated petitions were Nos. 80-1312, 80-1464, 80-1710 and 80-1712 in the United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit.
sections.Material Facts: On February 1, 1979, EPA proposed particulate standards for light duty diesel vehicles of 0.60 grams per mile for model year 1981 and 0.20 grams per mile for 1983. In the final rule, 45 Fed. Reg. 14,496 (1980), it kept the 0.60 standard but delayed it to 1982, set the 0.20 standard for 1985 to leave a margin for error, and set 0.26 grams per mile for light duty trucks. Diesels emit particulates at thirty to seventy times the rate of gasoline engines, and the main NOx control technique, exhaust gas recirculation, increases particulates. The 1985 standard depended on the trap oxidizer, a filter that periodically incinerates collected particulates. No filter material had yet survived the 50,000 mile useful life; the best test, a metal mesh trap on a GM Opel driven gently, lasted 12,800 miles at 55 percent efficiency. EPA also waived the statutory 1.0 gram per mile NOx standard for 1981 and 1982 diesels of five manufacturers.
sections.Procedural History: NRDC and the manufacturers petitioned for review of the particulate rule and the NOx waiver decisions under section 307 of the Clean Air Act. GM also petitioned EPA for reconsideration, which the agency denied at 45 Fed. Reg. 48,133 (1980). Challenges to application of the 1982 standard in California were held in abeyance after the California Air Resources Board modified its NOx standard. The cases were argued on October 28, 1980, before Judges Robb, Mikva and Ginsburg and decided on April 22, 1981. Judge Mikva wrote for the court, which upheld the regulations in their entirety. Judge Robb concurred in the NOx waiver holding and dissented from the approval of the 1985 particulate standard.
sections.Issue: Whether EPA's prediction that trap oxidizer technology would be available for 1985 model year vehicles was the product of reasoned decisionmaking, or crystal ball inquiry, under the arbitrary and capricious standard of section 307(d)(9)(A) of the Clean Air Act. Whether EPA properly identified its statutory authority and could set a single standard that even the worst performing diesel could meet rather than a stricter or graduated standard as NRDC urged. And whether EPA lawfully found that the NOx waivers would not endanger public health and that diesel technology had a potential for long term air quality benefit.
sections.Holding: The court upheld the particulate standards and the NOx waivers in full. It held that EPA had cited the wrong statutory provision, because section 202(a)(3)(A)(iii) mandated particulate standards only for heavy duty vehicles, but that the agency's health findings supported the same rule under section 202(a)(1), so no remand was needed. It held that EPA's prediction of technological availability met the requirement of reasoned decisionmaking because the agency identified the remaining problems of filter durability, efficiency and regeneration control and gave plausible reasons for believing each could be solved in the time available. It rejected NRDC's demands for a graduated or stricter standard as matters within EPA's regulatory discretion, and it sustained EPA's interpretation of the waiver criteria.
sections.Reasoning: Judge Mikva explained that the standard of review is the traditional arbitrary and capricious inquiry, but that predictions of future technology differ from assessments of existing technology. Congress intended EPA to press for the development of improved technology rather than be limited by what exists today, so if the agency were held to the certainty appropriate to current technology it could never set a standard until the technology was in hand. The court drew on International Harvester and National Lime for the principle that the agency must defend its methodology, but noted that statistical techniques for reviewing current data do not translate into rules for reviewing predictions of progress. The time element cut both ways: it added uncertainty, but the two to two and a half years each of design development and production lead time gave EPA leeway to adjust the standard later without the hardships of International Harvester, where production sequences had already begun. Applying its standard, the court found that EPA had answered GM's objections: many filter materials showed adequate initial efficiency, progress since 1978 had been rapid, durability testing was scarce only because researchers had first attacked more basic problems, the industry had itself projected 1985 as possible, throttling and heating elements were demonstrated regeneration methods, and microprocessor control was routine. On the waivers, the public health criterion focused on the waiver period, and EPA reasonably weighed slightly higher NOx against much lower particulates.

topics.lrs-n-technology-forcing: The diesel-emissions note accepts a reasoned technological prediction despite unresolved engineering work.
topics.lrs-n-hard-look: The court tests the agency’s explanation for confidence in a future technology without demanding present certainty.

learning.separateOpinions: Judge Robb concurred in Part III, upholding the NOx waivers, and dissented from Part II, sustaining the 1985 particulate standard. He accepted the majority's legal standard but concluded that the record did not offer plausible reasons for believing the durability problem could be solved in time: GM had tested materials from sixteen manufacturers since 1974, the best survived only 12,800 miles under gentle driving against a statutory useful life of 50,000 miles and an EPA goal of 100,000, and EPA's statement that a design could very likely be optimized within one and a half to two years was pious hope and speculation rather than evidence.
